Linear Algebra 00 and 01 worked with columns of numbers. This post asks what those columns have in common with polynomials, functions, matrices and the solutions of a differential equation — and answers with one definition: a vector space. From that definition come the ideas that organise the rest of the subject: subspaces, span, linear independence, basis and dimension. The central theorem is that dimension is well defined — every basis of a space has the same size — and it is proved here in full through the Steinitz exchange lemma. The abstract ideas are then brought back to matrices through Strang's four fundamental subspaces, with a complete worked example, a proof that row rank equals column rank, and the rank–nullity theorem in matrix form. The post ends with sums and direct sums of subspaces and the formula dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W−dim⁡(U∩W).
Series map: 00 Vectors & Linear Systems → 01 Matrix Algebra, Inverses & LU → 02 Vector Spaces, Basis & Dimension (this post) → 03 Linear Maps, Change of Basis & Determinants → 04 Eigenvalues & Diagonalization → 05 Inner Products, Spectral Theorem & SVD.

Field — a set F with an addition and a multiplication that satisfy the usual rules of arithmetic: both operations are associative and commutative, multiplication distributes over addition, there are elements 0≠1 with a+0=a and 1a=a, every a has a negative −a, and every nonzero a has an inverse a−1. Examples: Q, R, C, and F2={0,1} with arithmetic mod 2. The integers Z are not a field (2 has no integer inverse).
Scalars — the elements of the field. In this series F is R or C unless stated.
Everything in Linear Algebra 00 and 01 — elimination, pivots, inverses, LU — used only these field rules, so it works word for word over any field.

A vector space over F is a set V with an addition V×V→V and a scalar multiplication F×V→V such that, for all u,v,w∈V and a,b∈F:
u+v=v+u (commutativity).
(u+v)+w=u+(v+w) (associativity).
There is an element 0∈V with v+0=v for all v (additive identity).
For each v there is w with v+w=0 (additive inverse).
a(bv)=(ab)v.
1v=v.
a(u+v)=au+av.
(a+b)v=av+bv.
The elements of V are called vectors, whatever they actually are.

Proposition. In any vector space: (a) the zero vector is unique; (b) each v has exactly one additive inverse, written −v; (c) 0v=0; (d) a0=0; (e) (−1)v=−v.
Proof. (a) If 0 and 0′ are both identities, 0=0+0′=0′. (b) If w,w′ are both inverses of v, then w=w+(v+w′)=(w+v)+w′=w′. (c) 0v=(0+0)v=0v+0v; add −(0v) to both sides. (d) The same with a0=a(0+0). (e) v+(−1)v=(1+(−1))v=0v=0, so (−1)v is the inverse of v, by (b). ■

Space · Vectors · Operations
Fn · columns (x1,…,xn) · entry by entry
Pn(F) · polynomials of degree at most n · add coefficients; scale coefficients
P(F) · all polynomials · same
FS · all functions f:S→F on a set S · (f+g)(s)=f(s)+g(s), (af)(s)=af(s)

Fn is really the special case FS with S={1,…,n}: a column is a function from positions to numbers.
Non-examples. The first quadrant {(x,y):x,y≥0} fails axiom 4 — (1,0) has no inverse inside it. The line {(x,y):y=x+1} has no zero vector. The polynomials of degree exactly 2 are not closed under addition: (t2+t)+(−t2)=t.

Subspace — a subset U⊆V that is itself a vector space with the same addition and scalar multiplication.
Theorem (subspace test). A subset U of a vector space V is a subspace if and only if
0∈U;
u,w∈U⇒u+w∈U (closed under addition);
a∈F, u∈U⇒au∈U (closed under scalar multiplication).
Proof. A subspace clearly satisfies 2 and 3, and it contains its own zero vector z with z+z=z; adding −z in V shows z=0, so 1 holds. Conversely, suppose 1–3 hold. Conditions 2 and 3 make addition and scalar multiplication land in U. Axioms 1, 2, 5–8 are identities that hold for all vectors of V, so in particular for those of U. Axiom 3 holds by condition 1. For axiom 4: if u∈U then −u=(−1)u∈U by condition 3 and part (e) of the proposition. ■
Trick: conditions 2 and 3 together are the same as "closed under linear combinations": au+bw∈U for all u,w∈U and scalars a,b. Check 0 first — it is the fastest way to reject a non-subspace.

Null space N(A)={x∈Fn:Ax=0} is a subspace of Fn: A0=0, and A(au+bw)=aAu+bAw=0.
Column space C(A)={Ax:x∈Fn}, the span of the columns, is a subspace of Fm.
{p∈P2(R):p(1)=0} is a subspace; {p:p(1)=5} is not (no zero polynomial).
The symmetric n×n matrices form a subspace of Mn×n.
The solutions y of y′′+y=0 form a subspace of the twice-differentiable functions R→R.
The solutions of Ax=b with b≠0 are not a subspace (Linear Algebra 00, Chapter 7): 0 is not a solution.
The union of the x-axis and the y-axis in R2 is not a subspace: (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1) is in neither.
Intersections are subspaces. If U and W are subspaces, so is U∩W: it contains 0, and a linear combination of vectors in both lies in both. Unions usually are not, as the axes show; Chapter 8 replaces the union by the sum U+W.

The definitions from Linear Algebra 00 carry over unchanged. For a finite list v1,…,vk in V:
span⁡(v1,…,vk) is the set of all linear combinations a1v1+⋯+akvk. By convention the span of the empty list is {0}.
The list spans V if its span is all of V.
The list is linearly independent if a1v1+⋯+akvk=0 forces a1=⋯=ak=0; otherwise it is dependent. The empty list is independent.
Proposition. span⁡(v1,…,vk) is the smallest subspace of V containing every vi.
Proof. It contains 0, and a combination of combinations is a combination, so it is a subspace; it contains each vi. Any subspace containing all vi is closed under linear combinations, so it contains the span. ■

Lemma. If v1,…,vm is linearly dependent, then there is an index j such that
vj∈span⁡(v1,…,vj−1), and
removing vj from the list does not change its span.
Proof. Take a relation a1v1+⋯+amvm=0 with not all ai=0, and let j be the largest index with aj≠0. Then
vj=−a1ajv1−⋯−aj−1ajvj−1,
which proves 1. (If j=1 this says v1=0, the span of the empty list.) For 2, in any combination of the full list, replace vj by the right-hand side above; the result is a combination of the list without vj. ■

In P2(R), the list 1,t,t2 is independent: if a+bt+ct2 is the zero polynomial, all its coefficients are 0.
In the functions R→R, sin⁡ and cos⁡ are independent: if asin⁡x+bcos⁡x=0 for all x, then x=0 gives b=0 and x=π/2 gives a=0.
Common pitfall: "asin⁡x+bcos⁡x=0" means equality as functions, for every x. Finding one x where a combination is zero proves nothing; you must show the combination is zero everywhere only when all weights are zero.

Basis of V — a list of vectors in V that is linearly independent and spans V.
Finite-dimensional — V is spanned by some finite list. Otherwise infinite-dimensional.
Standard basis of Fn — e1,…,en. Of Pn(F) — 1,t,…,tn.
Theorem (unique representation). A list v1,…,vn is a basis of V if and only if every v∈V can be written as a1v1+⋯+anvn in exactly one way.
Proof. Spanning is "at least one way". If a basis gave two ways, subtracting them gives ∑(ai−bi)vi=0, so every ai=bi by independence. Conversely, uniqueness for v=0 (which is 0v1+⋯+0vn) is exactly independence. ■

Lemma (Steinitz exchange). Let V be a vector space. Suppose u1,…,um is linearly independent in V and w1,…,wn spans V. Then m≤n. Moreover, after renumbering the w's, the list
u1,…,um,wm+1,…,wn
also spans V.
Proof. We show by induction on k=0,1,…,m that k≤n and that, after renumbering, u1,…,uk,wk+1,…,wn spans V. For k=0 this is the hypothesis.
Assume it holds for some k<m. Since the list u1,…,uk,wk+1,…,wn spans V, we can write
uk+1=a1u1+⋯+akuk+bk+1wk+1+⋯+bnwn.
If every bj were 0 (in particular, if no w's were left, k=n), then uk+1 would be a combination of u1,…,uk, contradicting independence of the u's. So some bj≠0; hence k+1≤n. Renumber so that bk+1≠0 and solve for wk+1:
wk+1=1bk+1(uk+1−∑i=1kaiui−∑j=k+2nbjwj).
So wk+1 lies in the span of u1,…,uk+1,wk+2,…,wn. That span therefore contains the whole old spanning list, so it is V. This completes the step. At k=m we get m≤n and the stated spanning list. ■
Small example. In R3 take the independent u1=(1,1,0), u2=(0,1,1) and the spanning e1,e2,e3. Since u1=e1+e2 has a nonzero coefficient on e1, swap it out: u1,e2,e3 spans. Then u2=0 u1+e2+e3; swap out e2: u1,u2,e3 spans R3. (Three vectors that span R3 are automatically a basis — see the theorem at the end of this chapter.)

Theorem. In a finite-dimensional vector space, any two bases have the same length.
Proof. Let B1 and B2 be bases, of lengths m and n. B1 is independent and B2 spans, so m≤n by Steinitz. Swap roles: n≤m. ■
This common length is the dimension dim⁡V.
Space · Dimension · A basis
{0} · 0 · the empty list
Fn · n · e1,…,en
Pn(F) · n+1 · 1,t,…,tn
Mm×n(F) · mn · matrices with one entry 1, the rest 0
symmetric 2×2 · 3 · one basis matrix each for the (1,1), (2,2) and paired off-diagonal entries
P(F) · infinite · 1,t,t2,… (no finite list spans)
Watch out: Cn has dimension n over C but 2n over R (a basis over R is e1,ie1,…,en,ien). Dimension depends on the field of scalars.

Theorem. Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n.
Every spanning list can be shrunk to a basis by removing vectors.
Every independent list can be extended to a basis by adding vectors.
Any n independent vectors form a basis; any n spanning vectors form a basis.
Every subspace U is finite-dimensional with dim⁡U≤n, and dim⁡U=n only if U=V.
Proof. (1) While the list is dependent, the dependence lemma lets you remove one vector without changing the span. The process stops at an independent spanning list. (2) Apply Steinitz with a basis as the spanning list: the independent list plus the remaining n−m basis vectors spans V; it has length n, and by (1) some sublist is a basis, which must have length n, so it is the whole list. (3) An independent list of length n extends to a basis of length n, so nothing is added; a spanning list of length n shrinks to a basis of length n, so nothing is removed. (4) Any independent list in U is independent in V, so it has length at most n by Steinitz. Keep adding vectors of U not yet in the span of an independent list (independence is kept, by Exercise 7); this stops after at most n steps with a basis of U. If dim⁡U=n, that basis is n independent vectors of V, so by (3) it spans V, hence U=V. ■

If B=(v1,…,vn) is a basis of V, each v has unique weights with v=a1v1+⋯+anvn. The column [v]B=(a1,…,an)∈Fn is the coordinate vector of v relative to B.
The map v↦[v]B is one-to-one, onto Fn, and respects linear combinations: [au+bw]B=a[u]B+b[w]B. So every n-dimensional space over F behaves exactly like Fn, and computations in it can be done with columns and matrices. Linear Algebra 03 makes this precise (isomorphism) and studies how coordinates change when the basis changes.
Example in R2. With B=((1,1),(1,−1)) and x=(3,1): solve a(1,1)+b(1,−1)=(3,1), so a+b=3, a−b=1, giving a=2, b=1. So [x]B=(2,1), while the standard coordinates are (3,1) — same vector, different description.
Example in P2(R). With B=(1, 1+t, (1+t)2), find [t2]B. Put s=1+t; then t=s−1 and t2=s2−2s+1. So
t2=1⋅(1+t)2−2(1+t)+1⋅1,[t2]B=(1,−2,1)
(the weights on 1, 1+t and (1+t)2, in that order). Check: (1+2t+t2)−2−2t+1=t2.

For an m×n matrix A of rank r (the number of pivots):
Subspace · Symbol · Lives in · Definition
Column space · C(A) · Fm · all Ax; span of the columns
Null space · N(A) · Fn · all x with Ax=0
Row space · C(AT) · Fn · span of the rows
Left null space · N(AT) · Fm · all y with ATy=0, that is yTA=0T

Let EA=R with E invertible (a product of elementary matrices) and R the RREF.
Fact 1 — the row space does not change. Every row of R is a combination of rows of A, and since A=E−1R, every row of A is a combination of rows of R. So C(AT)=C(RT).
Fact 2 — linear relations among columns do not change. Ax=0 ⟺ EAx=0 ⟺ Rx=0, because E is invertible. So a combination of columns of A is zero exactly when the same combination of columns of R is zero, and N(A)=N(R). (The column spaces of A and R usually differ.)

C(A) — the pivot columns of A (not of R). In R the pivot columns are distinct standard basis vectors, so they are independent, and every other column is a combination of them. By Fact 2 the same holds for the corresponding columns of A.
C(AT) — the nonzero rows of R. They span the row space by Fact 1, and they are independent because each has a leading 1 in a column where the other rows have 0.
N(A) — the n−r special solutions (one free variable 1, the others 0), as in Linear Algebra 00.
N(AT) — the last m−r rows of E: those rows multiply A to give the zero rows of R.

Use the matrix from Linear Algebra 00, Chapter 6:
A=(1222246836810),R=(120−200120000),m=3, n=4, r=2.
Pivot columns 1 and 3; free variables x2,x4.
Column space (dimension r=2, in R3): basis (1,2,3) and (2,6,8) — columns 1 and 3 of A. The other columns satisfy the same relations as in R: column 2 =2× column 1, and column 4 =−2× column 1 +2× column 3. Check: −2(1,2,3)+2(2,6,8)=(2,8,10).
Row space (dimension r=2, in R4): basis (1,2,0,−2) and (0,0,1,2).
Null space (dimension n−r=2, in R4): basis s1=(−2,1,0,0) and s2=(2,0,−2,1).
Left null space (dimension m−r=1, in R3): the elimination steps R2−2R1, R3−3R1, R3−R2 make row 3 into −(row 1)−(row 2)+(row 3)=0. So y=(−1,−1,1) is a basis: yTA=0T.

Each row of A dotted with a null-space vector gives 0 — that is what Ax=0 says, one row at a time. So every vector of N(A) is orthogonal to every vector of C(AT). In the example, (1,2,0,−2)⋅(−2,1,0,0)=0, (1,2,0,−2)⋅(2,0,−2,1)=0, (0,0,1,2)⋅(−2,1,0,0)=0 and (0,0,1,2)⋅(2,0,−2,1)=0. In the same way N(AT) is orthogonal to C(A): (−1,−1,1)⋅(1,2,3)=0 and (−1,−1,1)⋅(2,6,8)=0. Over R the dimensions add up (2+2=4, 2+1=3), which makes each pair orthogonal complements — proved in Linear Algebra 05.

Theorem. For every matrix, dim⁡C(A)=dim⁡C(AT)=r, the number of pivots.
Proof. The pivot columns of A are a basis of C(A), and there are r of them. The nonzero rows of R are a basis of C(AT), and there are r of them (one per pivot). ■
This is not obvious: for a 3×100 matrix it says that the 100 columns span a space of the same dimension as the 3 rows. It also shows rank⁡A=rank⁡AT, and that r≤min⁡(m,n).
Rank-one matrices. A matrix has rank 1 exactly when it is a nonzero column times a nonzero row, A=uvT: every column is a multiple of u, every row a multiple of vT. The outer-product view of Linear Algebra 01 writes any AB as a sum of such pieces.

Theorem (rank–nullity). For an m×n matrix A,
dim⁡C(A)+dim⁡N(A)=n.
Proof. Let r be the number of pivots. dim⁡C(A)=r by Chapter 6. It remains to show that the n−r special solutions s1,…,sn−r are a basis of N(A).
Independent: look only at the free-variable entries. In sk the k-th free variable is 1 and the others are 0. So in ∑cksk the k-th free entry is ck; if the sum is 0, every ck=0.
Spanning: let x∈N(A) with free-variable values f1,…,fn−r. Then z=x−∑fksk is in N(A) and has every free variable equal to 0. The RREF expresses each basic variable in terms of the free ones, so all basic variables of z are 0 too; thus z=0 and x=∑fksk.
So dim⁡N(A)=n−r, and r+(n−r)=n. ■
In words: each of the n columns either contributes a pivot (a new direction in the column space) or a free variable (a new direction in the null space). For the example, 2+2=4. Applied to AT (which has m columns and the same rank), it gives dim⁡N(AT)=m−r, here 3−2=1.
The general version — for a linear map T:V→W, dim⁡V=dim⁡im⁡T+dim⁡ker⁡T — is proved in Linear Algebra 03.

Condition on the rank · Meaning for Ax=b
r=m (full row rank) · solvable for every b; C(A)=Fm
r=n (full column rank) · at most one solution; N(A)={0}
r=m=n · exactly one solution; A invertible
r<m and r<n · either no solution or infinitely many
For a square matrix, "rank n", "N(A)={0}" and "C(A)=Fn" join the invertible matrix theorem from Linear Algebra 01.
Trick: rank–nullity is a quick sanity check. A 5×7 matrix has rank at most 5, so its null space has dimension at least 7−5=2 — there are nonzero solutions of Ax=0 before any computation.

Sum of subspaces U,W⊆V: U+W={u+w:u∈U,w∈W}. It is the smallest subspace containing both (a subspace containing U and W contains all such sums).
Direct sum — the sum is direct, written U⊕W, if every vector of U+W can be written as u+w in only one way.
Proposition. U+W is direct if and only if U∩W={0}.
Proof. Suppose the sum is direct and v∈U∩W. Then 0=v+(−v) with v∈U, −v∈W, and also 0=0+0; uniqueness gives v=0. Conversely, if U∩W={0} and u+w=u′+w′, then u−u′=w′−w lies in both U and W, so it is 0. ■
Watch out: for three or more subspaces, pairwise zero intersections are not enough. Three distinct lines through the origin in R2 meet pairwise only at 0, but their sum is not direct (three vectors in R2 are dependent).

Theorem. If U and W are finite-dimensional subspaces of V, then
dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W−dim⁡(U∩W).
Proof. Let z1,…,zk be a basis of U∩W. Extend it to a basis z1,…,zk,u1,…,up of U and to a basis z1,…,zk,w1,…,wq of W (Chapter 4). The combined list z1,…,zk,u1,…,up,w1,…,wq clearly spans U+W. For independence, suppose
∑aizi+∑bjuj+∑clwl=0.
Then ∑clwl=−∑aizi−∑bjuj lies in W and in U, hence in U∩W, so ∑clwl=∑dizi for some di. The z's and w's together are a basis of W, so all cl=0 (and all di=0). Now ∑aizi+∑bjuj=0 is a relation in a basis of U, so all ai,bj=0. Hence the combined list is a basis, and
dim⁡(U+W)=k+p+q=(k+p)+(k+q)−k.■
This is the same shape as ∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣ for finite sets.

In R3, let U=span⁡(e1,e2) (the xy-plane) and W=span⁡(e2,e3) (the yz-plane). Then U∩W=span⁡(e2) and dim⁡(U+W)=2+2−1=3, so U+W=R3, but the sum is not direct.
The plane P={x:x1+x2+x3=0} and the line L=span⁡(1,1,1) satisfy P∩L={0} (a point (c,c,c) with 3c=0), so dim⁡(P+L)=2+1=3 and R3=P⊕L. For example (1,2,3)=(−1,0,1)+(2,2,2).
Every square matrix splits uniquely into symmetric plus skew-symmetric parts, M=12(M+MT)+12(M−MT), so over R or C (any field where 2≠0), Mn×n=Sym⊕Skew. For M=(1243) the parts are (1333) and (0−110).
For a real m×n matrix, Rn=C(AT)⊕N(A). The intersection is {0}, because a vector in both is orthogonal to itself, and x⋅x=0 forces x=0; the dimensions add to r+(n−r)=n. So every x∈Rn splits uniquely as x=xr+xn, a row-space part plus a null-space part — the left half of the four-subspace picture. Since Axn=0, Ax=Axr: every b in C(A) is Axr for a row-space vector xr, which is the arrow from row space to column space in the figure of Chapter 6.

Show that U={p∈P2(R):p(1)=0} is a subspace, and find a basis and its dimension.
Solution
The zero polynomial has p(1)=0, and (ap+bq)(1)=ap(1)+bq(1)=0, so U is a subspace. p(t)=c0+c1t+c2t2 is in U iff c0+c1+c2=0, i.e. c0=−c1−c2, so p=c1(t−1)+c2(t2−1). The list t−1, t2−1 spans U and is independent (only the second has a t2 term), so dim⁡U=2. This matches rank–nullity: U is the null space of the map p↦p(1), and 3−1=2.

Is {(x,y)∈R2:xy≥0} a subspace?
Solution
No. It contains 0 and is closed under scalar multiplication ((cx)(cy)=c2xy≥0), but not under addition: (1,0)+(0,−1)=(1,−1) has xy=−1<0. It is the union of the first and third quadrants.

Find a basis for span⁡{(1,2,1),(2,4,2),(1,0,1),(0,1,0)} taken from the given vectors, and its dimension.
Solution
Put them as columns and row reduce: (121024011210)→(1201/2001−1/20000). Pivot columns 1 and 3, so (1,2,1) and (1,0,1) are a basis and the dimension is 2. (All four vectors satisfy x1=x3, a plane.)

For B=(122436), give bases and dimensions of all four subspaces.
Solution
m=3, n=2, r=1 (B=(1,2,3)T(1,2)). C(B): (1,2,3), dimension 1. C(BT): (1,2), dimension 1. N(B): (−2,1), dimension n−r=1. N(BT): solutions of y1+2y2+3y3=0, basis (−2,1,0), (−3,0,1), dimension m−r=2. Check orthogonality: (1,2)⋅(−2,1)=0.

Find the coordinates of p(t)=2+3t+t2 relative to B=(1, 1+t, (1+t)2).
Solution
(1+t)2=1+2t+t2, so p−(1+t)2=1+t. Hence p=0⋅1+1⋅(1+t)+1⋅(1+t)2, and [p]B=(0,1,1). Check: (1+t)+(1+2t+t2)=2+3t+t2.

Let U and W be 3-dimensional subspaces of R5. Prove that U∩W≠{0}.
Solution
U+W⊆R5, so dim⁡(U+W)≤5. The dimension formula gives dim⁡(U∩W)=3+3−dim⁡(U+W)≥6−5=1.

Prove that if v1,…,vm is independent and v∉span⁡(v1,…,vm), then v1,…,vm,v is independent.
Solution
Suppose a1v1+⋯+amvm+av=0. If a≠0, then v=−1a∑aivi is in the span — a contradiction. So a=0, and then all ai=0 by independence of the vi. (This is the step used in Chapter 4, part 4.)

Linear Algebra 03 moves from spaces to maps between them. A linear map T:V→W is determined by what it does to a basis, so after choosing bases it becomes a matrix — and changing the bases changes the matrix to Q−1AP (or P−1AP for an operator). The post proves the full rank–nullity theorem for linear maps, defines isomorphism (why every n-dimensional space "is" Fn), and then builds the determinant from its defining properties, with its geometric meaning as a signed volume scale factor.

Kenneth Hoffman and Ray Kunze, Linear Algebra, 2nd edition, Prentice-Hall, 1971 — Chapter 2 (vector spaces, bases and dimension, coordinates, row-equivalence).
Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th edition, Wellesley-Cambridge Press, 2023 — Chapter 3 (the four fundamental subspaces, rank, dimensions).
Gilbert Strang, "The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra", The American Mathematical Monthly 100(9), 1993, pp. 848–855 — the source of the four-subspace picture.
David C. Lay, Steven R. Lay and Judi J. McDonald, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 6th edition, Pearson, 2021 — Chapter 4 (vector spaces, null and column spaces, bases, coordinate systems, dimension, rank).
MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2010 (Gilbert Strang) — Lectures 5–10: vector spaces, column and null spaces, solving Ax=0 and Ax=b, independence, basis and dimension, the four fundamental subspaces.
